358.title: A hundred years asleep
358.hook: a man passes a ruined town, dies a hundred years, and wakes to see his donkey raised (2:259)
358.carry: he can revive what is dead
358.howItsDone: Muslims read 2:258–260 together as three stories about God giving life to the dead, and often recall them when speaking of resurrection and of hope after loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no compulsion, and your line was the same two words. Did you let someone hold their view in peace? Today, a man who asks a hard question out loud, and is answered with a story he lives through. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

A traveler rides his donkey past a town that's been destroyed. Roofs fallen in, walls collapsed onto themselves, nobody left. He's carrying some food and something to drink. He stops, looks at the ruins, and says what anyone might say: how could God ever bring this back to life? The text doesn't say whether he asks it in wonder or in doubt. It's the question that comes standing in front of something truly finished. And then, the Qur'an says, he finds out. Today: a hundred years asleep.
screen: `A RUINED TOWN, NOBODY LEFT.` → `HOW COULD THIS EVER LIVE AGAIN?` → `THEN HE FINDS OUT.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred fifty-nine goes on: God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. And asked him: how long have you stayed? He answered: a day, or part of a day. That's how it feels to wake. No, a hundred years. Now look at your food and drink: they haven't spoiled. And look at your donkey. And look at the bones, how We set them together and then clothe them with flesh. And when it became clear to him, he said: I know that God has power over all things. The Qur'an doesn't name the man or the town. The commentators offer names: some say 'Uzayr, whom some identify with Ezra, and the town Jerusalem after its destruction; others name the prophet Jeremiah, or someone else. The text stays silent, and the story works without a name. Look at the details it does give. The food is unchanged after a century. The donkey, in one reading, has gone to bones and comes back; other commentators read the bones as the man's own. One thing time didn't touch, one thing it took completely, and in the story both are in God's hands. Now look where the story sits. Just before it, Ibrahim tells a king: my Lord gives life and causes death. Just after it, Ibrahim asks to see how the dead are raised, and is shown with four birds. Three stories in a row about the same question. The man's question isn't scolded. It's answered with a demonstration he lives through. He can revive what is dead.
screen: `A DAY, OR PART OF A DAY` · `THE FOOD UNSPOILED, THE DONKEY RAISED` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T NAME HIM` · `THREE STORIES, ONE QUESTION`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something old coming back to life. A tree putting out new leaves after winter. A friendship you thought was over that's started again. An old skill coming back to your hands. Bring one to mind and look at it closely: what was dead about it, and what's stirring now? If you pray, you can hold it up with the man's last words: I know that God has power over all things. The bell holds the time.
A hundred years asleep. The man who doubted a ruined town could live, was made to die a century, and woke to see his donkey raised. Today's word.
Your line: he can revive what is dead. Today, give one thing you'd written off, a plant, a hope, a friendship, one more look. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Seven ears of grain
359.hook: a gift in Allah's way is like a grain that grows seven ears, a hundred grains each (2:261)
359.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in amounts large and small, often citing 2:261 and the hadith that even a date given from honest earnings grows like a mountain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a hundred years asleep, and your line, he can revive what is dead. What did you give one more look? Today, life again, this time out of a single seed. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

Pull one stalk of wheat from a field and look at the top. The head, the ear, is packed with grains in neat rows. Any farmer knows the trade: you put one grain in the ground, and months later you hold dozens. It's arithmetic and hope in the same handful. Right after three stories about God bringing the dead to life, al-Baqarah turns to the field and does some arithmetic of its own. Today: seven ears of grain.
screen: `ONE STALK OF WHEAT.` → `ONE GRAIN IN, DOZENS OUT.` → `AL-BAQARAH DOES THE ARITHMETIC.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred sixty-one, in Pickthall's words: “The likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way is as the likeness of a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.” Do the math. One grain, seven ears, a hundred each: seven hundred. And the verse doesn't stop there. It adds: God multiplies for whom He wills. Seven hundred isn't the ceiling. The placement matters. The surah has just shown a dead town, a donkey's bones, four birds, all brought to life. Now a seed, buried and dead-looking, brings up a field. Giving is presented the same way: something you let go of into the ground, which looks lost, and comes back multiplied. Two hadith fill in the picture. A hadith qudsi in Bukhari and Muslim says a good deed is written as ten, up to seven hundred times, and many times more. And another hadith in Bukhari says that whoever gives even the value of a single date from honest earnings, God accepts it with His right hand and raises it the way one of you raises a young horse, until it becomes like a mountain. Notice the size of the gift in that hadith: one date. The grain in the verse is tiny too. Nothing in this passage asks for a large gift. It asks for a real one, given for God's sake, from what's honestly yours, and then let go. In the verse, the arithmetic is God's. One grain, seven hundred.
screen: `ONE GRAIN, SEVEN EARS, A HUNDRED EACH` · `NOT THE CEILING` · `BURIED, LOST-LOOKING, MULTIPLIED` · `ONE DATE BECOMES A MOUNTAIN`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a small amount today. Not a big decision. A coin, a dollar, a meal, ten minutes of help. Sit now, and choose where it goes: a charity, a neighbor, someone on the street, a colleague who's struggling. Picture handing it over and then letting it go, like a grain into the soil, without needing to see what grows. Hold that picture while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Seven ears of grain. Al-Baqarah's picture of giving: one grain that grows seven ears, a hundred grains each, and God multiplies further for whom He wills. Today's word.
Your line: one grain, seven hundred. Today, give the small thing you chose, and don't count what comes of it. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

360.title: Don't spoil it with reminders
360.hook: a kind word is better than charity followed by hurt (2:263–264)
360.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to give without reminding the recipient or expecting thanks; mann, recounting one's favors, is counted a serious fault, and many give quietly so as not to be tempted toward it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven ears of grain, and your line, one grain, seven hundred. Did you give the small thing? Today, al-Baqarah tells you how a gift can be lost after it's given. Day three hundred sixty.

Remember when I drove the truck? Remember who paid for the pizza? A relative helps someone move, years ago, and mentions it at every holiday since. The help was real: a whole Saturday, a borrowed truck, a sore back. But somewhere around the tenth reminder, the help starts to feel like a bill. The gift has turned into a debt that can never be paid off. Al-Baqarah knows this relative. Today: don't spoil it with reminders.
screen: `REMEMBER WHEN I DROVE THE TRUCK?` → `MENTIONED AT EVERY HOLIDAY.` → `A GIFT TURNED INTO A DEBT.`

segments.voice: Right after the seven ears of grain, the surah adds a condition. Verse two hundred sixty-two: those who spend and then don't follow it with reminders of their generosity, or with hurt, their reward is with their Lord. Verse two hundred sixty-three, in Pickthall's words: “A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury.” The Arabic for those reminders is mann: bringing up the favor, holding it over someone. Then verse two sixty-four gives the picture of what mann does. A smooth rock with a thin layer of soil on it. It looks like a field. Then heavy rain falls, and washes it bare. Nothing grows. That's a gift spoiled by reminders: it looked like soil, but there was only stone underneath. The very next verse paints the opposite. A garden on high ground. Heavy rain falls, and it doubles its fruit. And if no heavy rain comes, even a light drizzle is enough. That's the gift given for God's sake, with no strings: it grows whatever weather comes. The tradition takes mann seriously. A hadith in Sahih Muslim names three people God will not speak to on the Day of Judgment, and one of them is al-mannan, the one who reminds people of what he gave. Notice what the verse ranks above a spoiled gift: a kind word. You can give nothing at all, and say something gentle, and that's better than money with a sting. Give and forget.
screen: `NO REMINDERS, NO HURT` · `A KIND WORD IS BETTER` · `THE ROCK WASHED BARE` · `THE GARDEN ON THE HILL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give without mentioning it later. Sit, and think of something good you've done for someone that you've brought up since, out loud or in your head. The favor you keep score of. Picture it like a stone you've been carrying. Now picture setting it down by the road and walking on, without looking back. If you pray, you can leave it with God. If you don't, simply let it go. The bell holds the time.
Don't spoil it with reminders. Al-Baqarah's warning: reminders and hurt wash a gift away like rain off a rock; a kind word is better than a gift with a sting. Today's word.
screen: `DON'T SPOIL IT WITH REMINDERS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: give and forget. Today, do one kind thing, and don't mention it to anyone, including the person you did it for. Day three hundred sixty.

361.title: Write it down
361.hook: the longest verse is about recording debts fairly, with witnesses (2:282)
361.tomorrow: Not beyond what you can bear
361.howItsDone: Muslims draw on 2:282 for writing down loans and contracts with witnesses, and Islamic commercial law developed detailed rules for documentation from it; 2:280 adds the duty to give time to a debtor in hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't spoil it with reminders, and your line, give and forget. Did you do something kind and keep quiet about it? Today, the opposite instruction, for a different kind of money. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Two old friends. One lends the other a few thousand dollars, on a handshake, because writing it down would feel like distrust. A year later, one remembers it as a loan to be repaid by spring. The other remembers it as help, to be paid back someday. Neither is lying. The friendship doesn't survive the difference. What do you expect the longest verse in the Qur'an to be about? Heaven? The prophets? It's about this. Today: write it down.
screen: `A LOAN ON A HANDSHAKE.` → `TWO HONEST MEMORIES.` → `THE LONGEST VERSE IS ABOUT THIS.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred eighty-two, in Pickthall's words: “O ye who believe! When ye contract a debt for a fixed term, record it in writing.” Then the verse goes into detail, more detail than almost anywhere in the Qur'an. Let a scribe write it between you, in fairness, and let the scribe not refuse. Let the one who owes dictate, so the record is in the borrower's own words, and leave nothing out. If the borrower can't dictate, being of weak understanding, or weak, or unable, a guardian dictates fairly. Bring witnesses. Don't be too weary to write it down, small or large, with its due date. And the verse gives the reason: this is more just with God, more upright as testimony, and more likely to keep you from doubt. There's an exception for everyday trade, hand to hand on the spot: no harm if that's not written. And a protection: no scribe or witness is to be harmed for doing the job. Yesterday's lesson said: give and forget. Today's says: lend and write. They don't contradict. A gift should be forgotten by the giver. A debt should be remembered by both, exactly, so neither friendship nor faith is broken by a fuzzy memory. And just two verses earlier, al-Baqarah adds mercy to the record: if the one who owes is in hardship, give them time until it's easier, and if you let it go as charity, that's better for you. Write it down so it's fair; forgive it if they can't pay. Both sit a few lines apart in the same surah. Write it down.
screen: `RECORD IT IN WRITING` · `THE BORROWER DICTATES` · `GIVE AND FORGET; LEND AND WRITE` · `IN HARDSHIP, GIVE THEM TIME`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down something you owe. Not money only. A loan, yes, but also a returned favor, a promised visit, a book to give back, a reply someone's waiting for. Sit for a moment and let them surface. Choose one, and picture writing it clearly: what, to whom, by when. If you're the one owed, picture writing that down too, and decide whether, in someone's hardship, you'd give them time. The bell holds the time.
Write it down. The Qur'an's longest verse: record debts in writing, with a fair scribe and witnesses, so that nobody is wronged by a fuzzy memory. Today's word.
Your line: write it down. Today, put one thing you owe on paper, with a date, and keep it where you'll see it. Day three hundred sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 361 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NOT BEYOND WHAT YOU CAN BEAR.`

362.title: Not beyond what you can bear
362.word: Not beyond what you can bear
362.hook: Allah burdens no soul beyond its capacity, our Lord, forgive us (2:286)
362.carry: not beyond what I can bear
362.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah (2:285–286) every night before sleeping, following a hadith that they suffice whoever reads them at night; the requests of 2:286 are also said often in personal supplication.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a long verse about a debt, a scribe and witnesses. Your line was write it down. Did you write down something you owe? Day three hundred sixty-two, and the last day of al-Baqarah.

Al-Baqarah is two hundred eighty-six verses long. We've walked through it for almost a month: the cow, the Throne verse, no compulsion, a man asleep for a hundred years, a grain that becomes seven hundred, a debt written down. It holds laws, stories, warnings and arguments. And then, at the very end, it does something unexpected. It stops talking to people and turns into words people say back. The surah's last verse is a list of requests, and it opens with a promise about weight.
screen: `286 VERSES.` → `LAWS, STORIES, A DEBT.` → `THE END TURNS INTO A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, the verse opens: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The Arabic word for scope is wus'a, capacity, the room a thing has inside it. Every soul has a size, and the verse says what's asked of it fits inside. Then come the requests, each starting with our Lord. Don't take us to task if we forget or slip. Don't lay on us a burden like the one laid on those before us. Don't make us carry what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. There's a story behind it, in Sahih Muslim. When the verse just before, 2:284, came down, saying God will call people to account for what's in their hearts, whether they show it or hide it, the companions were frightened. They came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ on their knees and said this was more than they could carry. He told them to say instead: we hear and we obey. They said it, and then these last two verses came, the believers' answer and this list of requests. A related report in the same collection, from Ibn Abbas, says that after each request, God answered: I have done so. A second hadith, in Bukhari, says whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him. Scholars give different meanings for enough: enough protection, enough of a night prayer, or both. So the surah ends where some people end their day, in bed, saying these two verses. It doesn't promise that nothing will be heavy. It says the weight was measured to the one carrying it.
screen: `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE: WUS'A, CAPACITY` · `OUR LORD: A LIST OF REQUESTS` · `THE FRIGHTENED COMPANIONS` · `ENOUGH FOR THE NIGHT` · then, large: `ALLAH TASKETH NOT A SOUL BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: Tonight, if you'd like, read or recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah before you sleep, in Arabic or in a translation. For now, sit comfortably and let the bell start. Bring to mind one thing that feels heavy right now. Don't solve it. Just notice how big it is, and then notice that you are still here, holding it. On each out-breath, let the line be there: not beyond what I can bear. If you pray, you can add the verse's own words: our Lord, pardon us. The bell holds the time.
Not beyond what you can bear. God asks no soul more than its capacity, its wus'a, from the last verse of al-Baqarah. Today's word.
screen: `NOT BEYOND WHAT YOU CAN BEAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not beyond what I can bear. When something lands on you today, say the line once before you react, and remember the companions on their knees, and the answer that came. Day three hundred sixty-two.

363.title: Clear and ambiguous
363.hook: some verses are clear, the foundation, others open to many meanings (3:7)
363.carry: some verses are for sitting with
363.howItsDone: Muslim scholars read the Qur'an's clear (muhkam) verses as its foundation and interpret the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses in their light; many ordinary believers simply affirm that all of it is from God and leave hard verses to further study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last verse of al-Baqarah: no soul burdened beyond its capacity. Your line was not beyond what I can bear. Did you read the last two verses before sleep? Day three hundred sixty-three, and a new surah.

A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the first two long surahs a shared nickname: the two bright ones. Al-Baqarah, which we just finished, and Al 'Imran, the Family of Imran, which starts today. It's named for a family, the family of Imran, and it opens, almost at once, with a verse about reading itself. Before telling a single story, the surah stops to say: not every verse in this book works the same way. Some are meant to be clear. Some are meant to be lived with.
screen: `THE TWO BRIGHT ONES.` → `AL 'IMRAN: THE FAMILY OF IMRAN.` → `A VERSE ABOUT READING.`

segments.voice: Here's 3:7 in Pickthall's words. God has revealed the Scripture "wherein are clear revelations - they are the substance of the Book - and others (which are) allegorical." The clear verses are called muhkamat, from muhkam: made firm, tightly built. The root h-k-m also gives hikma, wisdom, and hakim, a judge. The verse calls these firm verses umm al-kitab, literally the mother of the Book: the foundation everything else rests on. The others are mutashabihat, verses that resemble one another, that can be read more than one way. Then the verse describes two kinds of readers. Those with a swerve in their hearts chase the ambiguous verses, looking for trouble and hunting for a hidden meaning. And those firmly rooted in knowledge say: we believe in it, all of it is from our Lord. Now here's a detail the commentators have long discussed. The verse says no one knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge. Where do you pause? If you stop after God, then only God knows the meaning, and the learned simply trust. If you read straight on, the learned know something of it too. Both readings have been held by respected scholars, and both pauses are known in recitation. Which verses count as ambiguous is discussed too: some name the letters that open certain surahs, some name verses about God's attributes, or the unseen. So the verse doesn't ask you to understand everything. It gives you a floor to stand on, and permission to leave some verses open, without forcing them.
screen: `MUHKAM: MADE FIRM` · `THE MOTHER OF THE BOOK` · `TWO KINDS OF READERS` · `WHERE DO YOU PAUSE?` · then, large: `ALL OF IT IS FROM OUR LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of a verse, or any line from any book, that you don't understand, or that troubles you a little. When the bell starts, bring it to mind and don't argue with it. Hold it the way you'd hold something fragile that isn't yours: loosely, with both hands. Then think of one line you do understand, one that's firm for you, and let that be the ground you sit on. Firm ground underneath, an open question in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Muhkam. Made firm, clear, tightly built. The muhkamat are the clear verses, the mother of the Book, from 3:7. Today's word.

Your line: some verses are for sitting with. Today, when something doesn't make sense right away, a sentence, a person, a situation, try leaving it open for an hour instead of deciding. Day three hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 363 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DON'T LET OUR HEARTS SWERVE.`

364.title: Don't let our hearts swerve
364.hook: our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You guided us (3:8)
364.howItsDone: Many Muslims say the supplication of 3:8, 'rabbana la tuzigh qulubana', after the daily prayers and in personal du'a, along with the Prophet's reported prayer to the Turner of hearts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, muhkam: the clear, firm verses, the mother of the Book, and others left open. Your line was some verses are for sitting with. Did you leave one thing open instead of deciding? Day three hundred sixty-four, the end of a week.

Yesterday's verse carried a warning: some people have a swerve in their hearts, and chase what's unclear. And the very next verse doesn't point a finger at them. It turns around and asks for help. Commentators hear the people who were just praised, those firmly rooted in knowledge, as the ones speaking. Their first worry isn't other people's hearts. It's their own. If anyone feels safe from drifting, it should be them. They don't.
screen: `A SWERVE IN THE HEART.` → `THE NEXT VERSE TURNS AROUND.` → `NOT THEIR HEARTS. OURS.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, 3:8 begins: "Our Lord! Cause not our hearts to stray after Thou hast guided us." Then it asks for mercy from God's own presence, and ends: You are the Bestower. Notice the link. Yesterday's verse said zaygh, a swerve, in the hearts of some. Today's asks la tuzigh, don't let them swerve. It's the same root, z-y-gh: to lean, to tilt away from straight. One verse describes the tilt; the next asks to be kept from it. Notice, too, the timing in the request: after You guided us. It isn't a prayer for people who are lost. It's for people who've already found the way and know that finding it once isn't the same as staying on it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported, in a hadith in Tirmidhi, to have often said: O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon your religion. Anas, who reports it, says the companions asked whether he feared for them, and he said yes: hearts are held between two of God's fingers, and He turns them as He wills. In the hadith's Arabic, Turner of hearts is muqallib al-qulub, and both words share one root, q-l-b, to turn over: the heart is named as the thing that turns. So the request is honest about how hearts work. Some Muslims say 3:8 in their own supplications after the prayer. And it closes a week that has been about keeping things: a man raised after a hundred years, a grain that multiplies, charity not spoiled by reminders, a debt written down, a burden that fits, verses held firm or held open. Today, a heart kept straight.
screen: `THE SWERVE, AND THE REQUEST` · `Z-Y-GH: TO TILT AWAY` · `AFTER YOU GUIDED US` · `QALB: THE THING THAT TURNS` · then, large: `OUR LORD! CAUSE NOT OUR HEARTS TO STRAY.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you can say 3:8 after your next prayer, in Arabic or in your own language: rabbana la tuzigh qulubana. For now, when the bell starts, sit up straight, and feel how small the movements are that keep you upright: a lean forward, a correction back. Nobody sits perfectly still. Think of one place this week where your heart tilted a little, toward impatience, envy, or carelessness. Don't scold it. Just notice the lean, and come back to center. The bell holds the time.
Don't let our hearts swerve. The request of 3:8, made by people already guided, asking to stay that way. Today's word.
screen: `DON'T LET OUR HEARTS SWERVE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep my heart straight. Today, when you notice yourself leaning, toward a sharp word or an old habit, take that as the moment to correct, not to give up. Day three hundred sixty-four.

myth: 3:8 is a prayer for people who are lost
it asks God not to let hearts swerve after You guided us: it's for people already on the way.
3:7 and 3:8 share the root z-y-gh
one describes a swerve in the heart; the next asks to be kept from it.
the Prophet never worried about his own heart
Tirmidhi reports he often asked the Turner of hearts to keep his heart firm.

fork.setup: you've just heard a verse warning about people whose hearts swerve. the next verse is spoken by the faithful. what do they say?
options: at least we're not like them.
our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after You guided us.
explain the hard verses to us now.
fork.reveal: they ask for their own hearts to be kept straight. the verse turns from describing others to a request about ourselves.

original.note: Arabic: our Lord, do not let our hearts swerve (3:8).

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer to be shown the way.
what it means: a prayer by people already guided, asking not to drift from it.
what a scholar hears: la tuzigh answers the zaygh of 3:7, the same root; and qalb, heart, from a root about turning, echoed in the hadith of the Turner of hearts.
